clue.text: After bank holiday, go off to take up caring role

definitions.note: a role standing for the person who fills it

parts.note: 1 January, New Year's Day, is a UK bank holiday, written JAN I

indicators.note: in a down entry, taking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: food that goes off rots

explanation.surface: Someone back from a bank holiday decides to slack off by starting a care job.
explanation.walkthrough: A bank holiday is a UK public holiday; New Year's Day is one, and its date is written as the month abbreviation plus Roman one. 'Go off' means spoil, not leave.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor is a caretaker, someone whose job is looking after a building.

clue.text: Gun on grouse moor expects to attract disapproval

definitions.note: read as a phrase: what a shooter hopes to do
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gun, a member of a shooting party, hopes to bag a grouse
second meaning: an idiom for being booed or hissed

explanation.surface: A shooter on a Scottish moor is sure to draw criticism from opponents of blood sports.
explanation.walkthrough: In British shooting a 'gun' is a person, not the weapon. The phrase 'expects to' links the literal sense to the idiom, so the clue also reads as a whole comment on grouse shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the bird is a theatre idiom for being hissed at, so it means meeting with public disapproval.

clue.text: Humour about the origin of religion that may be holy

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: wit is clever humour

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it starts, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of religion

explanation.surface: A dry remark about how a religion began.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the phrase Holy Writ: the answer is a word that can follow 'Holy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Holy Writ is a name for sacred scripture, so writ is a word that may be described as holy.

clue.text: Role in clinic is plain

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: SAN is short for sanatorium, a clinic for convalescents
an actor's role is a part

explanation.surface: Someone's job at a medical clinic is unremarkable.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartan means austere and simple, without comfort or decoration, like life in ancient Sparta.

clue.text: Result of huge explosion, rubble can spread round area

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go around another piece
spread suggests the letters are scattered and laid out anew

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: After a big blast, debris can fly over a wide area.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes a demolition, but the explosion meant is a supernova.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crab Nebula is the cloud of gas left by a supernova observed in 1054.

clue.text: A month going up one of many English rivers

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: NOV is the abbreviation for November

explanation.surface: A month in which the level rises on one of England's many rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Several English rivers are called Avon, from a Celtic word for river, so it is one of many.

clue.text: Overturn limit on dimensions

parts.note: a cap is an upper limit
size is a thing's dimensions; on joins it to the cap

explanation.surface: A call to overturn a restriction on how big something can be.
explanation.definitionFit: To capsize is to overturn, used mainly of a boat turning over in the water.

clue.text: Celebrity given sack, so show off

parts.note: a big name is a celebrity
to drop someone is to sack them

explanation.surface: A star is fired and so makes a scene.
explanation.definitionFit: To name-drop is to mention famous acquaintances to impress others, a form of showing off.

clue.text: Have great fun taking in a show

indicators.note: taking in means one piece swallows another inside it

parts.note: to revel is to make merry
taken as written

explanation.surface: Enjoying a night out at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like the noun from the surface, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal is to show something that was hidden, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Corruption by some police repelled autocrat

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back, so the string is read backwards

parts.note: rot is moral decay
by and at both mean next to, as in at the door
the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police

explanation.surface: A tyrant who fended off a police corruption inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repelled' turns round the whole run of three pieces, not just the last one. 'Some police' points to the detective branch of British police.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictator rules with absolute power, which is exactly what an autocrat does.

clue.text: Mistake about an exile

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: bish is British slang for a blunder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A blunder concerning someone sent away from their homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exile' reads as a noun after 'an', but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To banish someone is to send them away from their country, which is to exile them.

clue.text: Prestige award no. 1 to pair on exercise in tropical land

indicators.note: in places the group inside a country's name
on means placed after, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: the abbreviation itself, minus its full stop
a Central American country in the tropics
physical education
an ace counts as one in cards
PR is the abbreviation for pair

explanation.surface: A top award going to a couple working out in the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No. 1' reads as a single ranking, but it splits: the abbreviation gives NO and the digit gives ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel Peace Prize is among the most prestigious international honours.

clue.text: Make to kill germs: across your vision, in your ears

definitions.note: read as: treat to kill germs

indicators.note: what lands in your ears is heard, so the phrase is judged by sound

parts.note: across your field of vision is past your eyes

explanation.surface: A garbled instruction about germs, sight and hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: Something moving across your vision goes past your eyes, and that phrase said quickly gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasteurising, named after Louis Pasteur, heats milk or other liquids to destroy harmful bacteria.

clue.text: Four smashing trophies, staggering! (That's bloody descriptive)

indicators.note: smashing into something means breaking in, so one piece goes inside
something staggering lurches about unsteadily, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An exclamation of amazement at four trophies being broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' looks like a British swear word, but it is literal: the answer describes blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Rh positive describes blood carrying the rhesus factor, so it is a term that characterises blood.

clue.text: One pelted round small city

indicators.note: round means wrapping around another piece

parts.note: a mink is an animal prized for its pelt
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Someone pelted with stones around a small town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pelted' suggests being bombarded, but here it means having a pelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Minsk is the capital city of Belarus.

clue.text: Partner's catching Papa's disease

indicators.note: catching means grabbing and holding something inside

parts.note: Mum is Dad's partner; the possessive is read as is
Papa is P in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A wife caught her husband's illness.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Partner's' is read as 'is', MUM'S without its apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumps is a contagious viral disease causing swollen glands in the neck.

clue.text: In early summer, spin round English tree

parts.note: June 1, written JUN I, is a date early in the summer

indicators.note: round means going around another piece

parts.note: public relations, the trade in spin
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Spinning around an English tree on an early summer day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In early summer' is a date, the first of June, not a time phrase. Spin in the political sense is PR.
explanation.definitionFit: The juniper is an evergreen coniferous tree or shrub whose berries flavour gin.

clue.text: Holmes is in Imogen's farm

parts.note: Imogen is the setter, so the setter's is my
a croft is a small farm, mainly in Scotland

explanation.surface: The setter claims Sherlock Holmes lives on their farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holmes' suggests Sherlock, but the answer is his elder brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Mycroft Holmes is Sherlock's brother in Conan Doyle's stories, so the surname alone can stand for him.

clue.text: Very incisive state of mind, or the opposite

definitions.text: state of mind, or the opposite

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for very
acuity is sharpness of mind

explanation.surface: A sharp mental state, or its reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition shares words with the wordplay: 'state of mind' feeds ACUITY, while 'state of mind, or the opposite' of incisive defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Vacuity is emptiness of mind, a lack of intelligence, the opposite of sharp insight.

clue.text: Old invader wanting ready rewards, fighting in this?

parts.note: the Huns invaded Europe in the 4th and 5th centuries

indicators.note: fighting suggests a scuffle that throws the letters into disorder

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A mercenary invader of old wants quick payment for battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fighting' does double duty: it scrambles the letters and, with 'in this?', points to a war.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hundred Years' War was the long series of conflicts between England and France, 1337 to 1453.

clue.text: Fish out of water, or one on the bed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a smoked herring, a fish no longer in the sea
second meaning: someone having a kip, a nap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish out of water' suggests the idiom for someone ill at ease, and 'bed' a river bed; both are red herrings. Kip is British slang for sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A kipper is a split, smoked herring, and a kipper is also someone who kips, or sleeps.

clue.text: Great discomfort to be expected at a French breakfast

definitions.text: to be expected at a French breakfast
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the French word for bread

explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes that breakfast in France is an ordeal; the second meaning is French bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain is English for severe discomfort and French for bread, a breakfast staple.

clue.text: Among engineers, Turing failed to convince

indicators.note: among means placed in the middle of something

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

indicators.note: a failed thing has broken down, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Alan Turing could not persuade his fellow engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that rings true sounds genuine, so it convinces those who hear it.

clue.text: They don't approve the hooter being sounded

indicators.note: being sounded means said out loud, so the word is judged by how it is heard

parts.note: hooter is slang for the nose

explanation.surface: Objectors who dislike a car horn being honked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooter' suggests a horn, but it is slang for the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The noes are those voting against a motion, as in 'the noes have it'.

clue.text: Class contains one who is far ahead of the rest

definitions.text: one who is far ahead of the rest

indicators.note: contains means holding something inside

parts.note: a genus is a class in biological classification
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A class includes a pupil who outshines everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class' suggests a school class; strictly a genus is a rank well below a class in taxonomy, so the match is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A genius has exceptional intelligence, putting them far beyond their peers.

clue.text: Veto? It's your choice

parts.note: surface reading: someone asks whether to block a decision
setter's reading: the answer, taken as a clue itself, would rearrange its last four letters into the first word

explanation.surface: Someone is told the power to block a proposal is entirely theirs.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: read FREE as a shuffle signal and VOTE as its letters and you get VETO. 'It's your choice' is the plain meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A free vote in Parliament lets members follow their own conscience instead of the party whip.
